transcription.text: Yeah, I first learned, Derek, I first learned about the benefit of that back in 1989 at my first job,
and I couldn't believe it when I had a HP, I can't remember what model, but it was a HP
six and a half digit rack meter, and it was in a rack, like it was like in my cubicle,
right, I had my cubicle, had my rack, because like I was testing lots of rack mount stuff,
like it was rack mount thing, and I needed other rack mount test systems and stuff,
because I was a repair and test tech, and yeah, so we had a HP six and a half digit meter in there,
and I discovered that it was brilliant for tracing down shorts, you know, because I was only young,
you know, I'd never had this sort of precision meter before, I'm used to my three and a half
digit multimeter, right, or my analog multimeter before that, like, and I just discovered that
it was so useful for tracking down, like, because a lot of the stuff I was, a lot of stuff I was
repairing was brand new produced rack mount boards, like giant 19 inch rack boards, so they're like,
you know, giant rack boards like this, right, full of TTL chips, like hundreds of TTL chips,
and yeah, like you'd get, like, so they come out of the wave solder machines, and you know,
the clearance on that, you get shorts between pins and ground planes and all sorts of things,
it was very common to get shorts on these boards, so I learned very quickly that this six and a half
digit meter was brilliant for finding short, you know, I could, like, get really sharp, nice probes
and put one here and go here, and I could narrow down the location of the short using, you know,
even though the ohms measurement wasn't accurate, who cared, right, the fact that it, the value got
lower because you could see the digits on there, it got lower and lower and lower as you got closer
to the short, and I nailed hundreds of shorts that way, it's great, highly recommended, just for that
use alone, yeah, it's great.
